examples.problem_statement: A 10-student class is to choose a president, vice president, and secretary from the group. Assuming that no person can occupy more than one post, in how many ways can this be accomplished?

solution.description: Ask how many choices exist for the first post. Since no one has been chosen yet, all 10 students are available for president.
Move to vice president. One student is already committed as president, so only 9 students remain eligible for this post.
Move to secretary. Two students are now taken by the earlier posts, leaving 8 students to choose from.
Apply the fundamental counting principle: multiply the independent per-post choice counts together to get the total number of possible selections.

key_reminders: The fundamental counting principle: multiply the number of choices available at each stage to get the total number of outcomes.
Because no person can occupy more than one post, each selection reduces the pool available to the next post by one.
Order matters here, since the three posts are distinct roles rather than an unlabeled group.
common_mistakes: Treating the three posts as an unordered group and dividing by 3!, which gives 120 instead of 720.
Reusing 10 for every post (10^3 = 1000) by forgetting that a chosen student is removed from the pool.

examples.problem_statement: j + 2k > 0 and j - k < 3. Quantity A: k. Quantity B: -1. Choose (A) Quantity A is greater, (B) Quantity B is greater, (C) The two quantities are equal, or (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: \text{two inequalities whose signs point in opposite directions}
solution.description: Recognize the setup: two variables and two inequalities can often be combined by adding them, but adding is only legitimate once both inequality signs face the same direction, and here they do not.
Multiply everything in the second inequality by -1, which flips the inequality sign so that both inequalities now point the same way.
Add the two same-direction inequalities term by term; j cancels against -j, leaving a statement in k alone.
Divide both sides by the positive number 3, which leaves the inequality direction unchanged, to isolate k.
Compare the quantities: because k must be greater than -1 in every case allowed by the constraints, Quantity A is always greater.

key_reminders: Two inequalities may be added only when both signs face the same direction.
Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction; dividing by a positive number does not.
In quantitative comparison, choose (A) only if the derived relationship holds for every value permitted by the constraints.
common_mistakes: Adding j + 2k > 0 and j - k < 3 as printed, without first flipping the second sign, which yields the invalid conclusion k > -3 with j uncancelled.
Multiplying the second inequality by -1 but leaving the sign as < , producing -j + k < -3 and the reversed comparison.
Concluding (D) on the grounds that j and k are individually unknown, even though j cancels and k is fully bounded.
